title: Life Begins
summary: The sperm and the egg (ovum) unite by fertilisation; the fertilised ovum is the zygote. It attaches to the lining of the uterus and grows by drawing nutrition from the mother; it is called a foetus until birth and a baby afterwards. Signs of pregnancy: a missed menstrual period (the first indication), morning sickness or nausea, enlarged tender breasts with darker areola, increased frequency of urination towards the end, and cravings (sweets, spicy or sour food; inedible things like mud or chalk need a doctor) or aversion to certain foods and smells. The father's chromosome decides the sex of the baby.

The foetus stays in the womb about nine months (280 days) – the prenatal period. Expected date of delivery = first day of the last menstrual period + 7 days + 9 months (for example, January 1, 2012 gives October 8, 2012; an approximate date). The nine months are three trimesters of three months. First trimester (0–3 months): the fertilised egg divides, attaches to the uterus and becomes an embryo with life-support systems (amniotic sac, placenta, umbilical cord); heart and lungs form and the circulatory system works; the embryo becomes a foetus with a human form. Second trimester (3–6 months): rapid growth in size and very fast brain development; the mother feels movements; a 6-month foetus cannot survive if born. Third trimester (6–9 months): continued growth; the foetus regulates breathing and body temperature and sucks its thumb; in the eighth month it gets antibodies from the mother.

Factors affecting the foetus: mother's emotional state (avoid stress); mother's diet (rice or wheat, pulses, eggs, green leafy vegetables and fruits, milk; avoid excess ghee and oil); age of mother (20–35 years is right; below 20 the body is not developed, risk of a weak child and miscarriage; keep a gap of at least 3 years between children); medicines (can pass through the placenta; take only on the doctor's advice; avoid X-rays); diseases (German measles, STIs, HIV pass the placenta); drugs, alcohol and smoking (pass into the foetus's blood; avoid sitting in a room where someone smokes).

Medical check-up: register with a doctor or health centre (in villages through an ASHA or Anganwadi worker); tests – haemoglobin (anaemia), blood group, blood sugar (diabetes), VDRL (STIs) and HIV; weight measured; tetanus injection; visit once a month for the first 8 months and once a week in the last month. Ultrasound checks growth, but misuse to find the sex and abort a female foetus is female foeticide; every child has the right to be born. Nutrition: balanced diet with regular meals; for morning sickness eat dry toast, biscuit or puffed rice in the morning; iron-rich foods (whole cereals, pulses, green leafy vegetables, jaggery, amla, liver) prevent anaemia; fruits, raw vegetables and fluids prevent constipation; avoid spicy and fried foods (acidity); small frequent meals; last meal 2–3 hours before sleep; myths and superstitions about foods should be avoided. Weight: normal gain is about 12 kg. Medicines: only under a doctor; two doses of tetanus toxoid (the second a month after the first) to protect the newborn; iron and folic acid supplements. Clothes: loose, comfortable (kurta-salwar, sari). Exercise and rest: continue normal work, avoid heavy lifting, at least 10 hours of sleep; family support.

Institutional delivery (hospital, primary health centre, registered nursing home) is safest; otherwise a trained midwife or dai. Five rules of cleanliness: clean hands and fingernails; clean surface; clean sheet; clean all items with antiseptic and soap; cord cut with a new blade and tied with new thread. After birth the newborn sleeps about 16 hours a day. Postnatal period is sometimes called the fourth trimester. Hygiene: wipe the baby with a clean cloth in warm water without scrubbing the protective white coating; keep the cut cord dry and uncovered (cover lightly if flies and dust); the mother keeps her room clean, well-lit and ventilated, bathes regularly and keeps stitches clean and dry. Immunisation: BCG and oral polio at birth; DPT and oral polio at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; hepatitis B; MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) at 9–12 months; boosters; vitamin A; free at government hospitals and health centres; pregnant women get tetanus toxoid.

Nutrition: put the baby to the breast within the first hour; colostrum, the yellowish first milk, gives antibodies and protein; exclusive breast milk for six months, supplementary foods can start after four months. Breast feeding compared with bottle feeding: adequate nutrients and easily digested; clean and reduces diarrhoea; always the right temperature; contains antibodies; builds an emotional bond. Bottle milk may be wrongly diluted, bottles must be sterilised, temperature must be adjusted, no protective agents, less bonding. Working mothers can express milk into sterilised bottles; maternity leave is 6 months and paternity leave 15 days (government). Family planning: parents decide when and how many children; a small family gives the mother more time and energy and money for children's needs; large families born one after another affect the mother's health. In an unplanned pregnancy only the woman decides whether to continue; she should consult a doctor and counsellor.

objective: State True or False: (i) One should not scrub the skin of a newborn child. (ii) On an average a pregnant woman should gain 12 kg weight. (iii) Women should not have a bath for a week after delivery. (iv) BCG vaccine should be given after 6 months of birth.
(i) True – the white coating and fine hair are protective. (ii) True. (iii) False – she should bathe regularly. (iv) False – BCG is given at birth.

State True or False: (i) Breast milk is the healthiest food as it fulfils all the nutritional needs of the infant. (ii) Colostrum is good for the baby. (iii) The mother should not breast feed for the first few days. (iv) Breast-fed babies are stronger and healthier.
(i) True. (ii) True. (iii) False – the baby should be put to the breast within one hour. (iv) True.

Fill in the blanks: (i) Pregnant women must take ______ vaccination. (ii) The first trimester of pregnancy begins with ______. (iii) Medicines can pass through the ______ and enter the baby's body. (iv) Protein is required by a pregnant woman for her own ______ development.

Fill in the blanks: (i) The age of the mother between ______ and ______ years is right for a baby. (ii) The gap between two children should be at least ______ years. (iii) Care of a woman during pregnancy is ______ care. (iv) A newborn sleeps about ______ hours a day.
Match the vaccine with the disease: (i) BCG (ii) Oral polio (iii) DPT (iv) MMR; (a) diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus (b) polio (c) tuberculosis (d) measles, mumps, rubella.

Match the trimester with a feature: (i) First (ii) Second (iii) Third (iv) Fourth; (a) fast brain growth and movements felt (b) heart and lungs form (c) foetus gets antibodies from mother (d) postnatal period.

State True or False: (i) Smoke from a cigarette can pass into the foetus's blood through the placenta. (ii) A pregnant woman may take any medicine without asking a doctor. (iii) Ultrasound is used to check the growth of the foetus. (iv) Misuse of ultrasound to find the sex causes female foeticide.

State True or False: (i) Bottle-fed milk contains protective antibodies. (ii) Bottles need to be sterilised. (iii) Exclusive breast milk is best for the first six months. (iv) Working mothers cannot give their milk to babies.
(i) False. (ii) True. (iii) True. (iv) False – they can express and store the milk in sterilised bottles.
vsa: Tell four reasons why regular medical check-up is important during pregnancy.

It confirms pregnancy and checks the growth of the foetus; routine tests (haemoglobin for anaemia, blood group, blood sugar, VDRL and HIV) detect problems early; weight is monitored and the tetanus injection and iron-folic acid supplements are given; complications can be handled in time for a safe delivery.

As an Asha worker make the women aware of four signs that confirm pregnancy.
Missed menstrual period; morning sickness or nausea; enlarged, tender breasts with darker nipple area; frequent urination; cravings for or aversion to certain foods.

What are the five disadvantages of bottle feeding? (give four)

The milk may be wrongly diluted and hard to digest; bottles that are not sterilised cause infections and diarrhoea; the temperature of the milk must be adjusted; it has no protective antibodies; it does not form a special bond between mother and baby.

Suggest any four ways of taking post-delivery care of a woman.

Keep her room clean, well-lit and ventilated; regular bath and clean, dry stitches; balanced nutritious diet and fluids; adequate rest and family support; check-ups; protect her from infections; emotional support.
April 2023
Write any four factors that affect the growing foetus.
Mother's emotional state; mother's diet; age of the mother; medicines taken; diseases like German measles, STIs and HIV; drugs, alcohol and smoking.
Calculate the expected date of delivery for a woman whose last menstrual period began on June 15, 2009.
Expected date of delivery = first day of last menstrual period + 7 days + 9 months. June 15 + 7 days = June 22, 2009; adding 9 months gives March 22, 2010.
What are the possible ill effects of having a child before 20 years of age?
The reproductive system is not fully developed, so there may be complications in delivery, a physically or mentally weak child, risk to the lives of mother and child, and risk of miscarriage.
Why is a pregnant woman advised to take tetanus vaccination? How many doses?
To protect the newborn from tetanus. Two doses are taken: the first as early as possible and the second one month after it; a booster within 3 years.
sa: Why is it important for a baby to be breast fed? Tell six reasons.

Breast milk has all the nutrients in the right proportion and is easily digested; colostrum gives antibodies and proteins that protect from infection; it is clean and reduces diarrhoea; its temperature is always right; it improves immunity so babies are healthier and stronger; it builds an emotional bond between mother and child; it is free and always available.
Trace the development of the foetus in the three trimesters.

First trimester (0–3 months): the fertilised egg divides, attaches to the uterus and becomes an embryo with amniotic sac, placenta and umbilical cord; heart and lungs form and the foetus attains a human form. Second trimester (3–6 months): rapid growth, very fast brain development, movements can be felt, but a 6-month foetus cannot survive outside. Third trimester (6–9 months): the foetus grows, can regulate breathing and body temperature and suck its thumb, and in the eighth month it gets antibodies from the mother to prepare for life outside.
Write any four points on the care of a newborn baby's cord and skin, and two on immunisation.

Wipe the baby with a clean cloth in warm water and do not scrub, because the white coating and fine hair are protective; keep the cut cord dry and open to air and cover it lightly only if there are flies and dust. Immunise on time: BCG and oral polio at birth, DPT at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, MMR at 9–12 months; it is free at government hospitals and health centres.
la: Explain how a pregnant woman should be cared for during pregnancy (five points).

(1) Register with a doctor or health centre and go for monthly check-ups with routine tests and the tetanus injection. (2) Take a balanced nutritious diet in small frequent meals; iron-rich foods against anaemia; dry toast for morning sickness; avoid spicy and fried foods. (3) Weigh herself regularly; an average gain of 12 kg is normal. (4) Take medicines only on a doctor's advice and avoid X-rays, smoking, alcohol and drugs. (5) Wear loose comfortable clothes, continue normal work, avoid heavy lifting, and get at least 10 hours of sleep with support and a stress-free environment from the family.
Discuss why family planning is important and compare breast feeding with bottle feeding in any three points.

Family planning lets parents decide when to start a family and keep an adequate gap between children; the mother stays healthy, has time and energy for each child and the family can spend more on education and entertainment, while children born in quick succession get less attention and nutrition. Breast feeding: nutrients are adequate and easily digested; it is clean and always at the right temperature; it gives antibodies and bonding. Bottle feeding: nutrients depend on dilution; bottles must be sterilised and the temperature adjusted; no protective agents and less bonding.
